blocks.text: Segment trees generalize to any ASSOCIATIVE aggregate function, and min/max are the second most common choice after sum. This topic focuses on why min and max fit the segment tree model, and the one critical detail that changes when adapting sum segment tree code to min or max.

The most common bug when adapting a sum segment tree to min or max: using the WRONG identity element for the completely outside case. Getting this wrong silently produces incorrect results with no error at all.

content.title: 1. Why Min and Max Fit the Segment Tree Model

blocks.caption: Each internal node stores the minimum of its two children, exactly analogous to how a sum segment tree stores the sum.
blocks.alt: Why Min and Max Fit the Segment Tree Model

blocks.text: min(min(a,b), c) equals min(a, min(b,c)), the associative property. A parent's min is simply the min of its two children's mins, exactly analogous to how a parent's sum is the sum of its children's sums in the sibling sum topic.

blocks.caption: Each aggregate function needs its own identity element for the completely outside base case: 0 for sum, positive infinity for min, negative infinity for max.

blocks.text: For SUM, the identity returned when a node is entirely outside the query range is 0. For MIN it must be POSITIVE INFINITY (or INT_MAX), and for MAX it must be NEGATIVE INFINITY (or INT_MIN). The identity element for any aggregation must be a value that, when combined with any real result via the aggregate operation, does not change that result.

0 works for addition but would incorrectly become the returned minimum or maximum if mistakenly used as the identity for a min or max query, since 0 is a perfectly ordinary value that could be smaller than every real element in the array.

Computing a range MINIMUM query follows the exact same outside/inside/partial overlap recursion structure as sum. The only behavioral difference: at an outside node, the algorithm returns positive infinity instead of 0, and since min(anything, positive infinity) equals anything, that identity value is effectively ignored once combined with a real result from a sibling branch.

This is structurally near identical to a sum segment tree, only addition is replaced with min() and 0 is replaced with INT_MAX. Maximum is the exact mirror: min() becomes max(), and INT_MAX becomes INT_MIN. This near identical structure is not a coincidence, it is the associativity that matters, not the specific operation chosen.

A genuinely distinct harder variant asks not just for the minimum VALUE in a range, but the INDEX at which that minimum occurs. The implementation change: each node stores a PAIR, the min value AND the index where it occurs, and when combining two children, compare their min VALUES but propagate the INDEX belonging to whichever child had the smaller value.

Build is O(n), query is O(log n), the identical bounds as the sum variant, since the asymptotic behavior comes from the tree's structure and the outside/inside/partial recursion pattern, not from which specific associative operation is being combined.

Using 0 as the identity for a min or max query: the single most common and subtle bug when adapting sum segment tree code, since it compiles and often even LOOKS correct on test cases where the real minimum happens to be less than 0 is never actually reached.
Forgetting a max segment tree's identity must be negative infinity, not positive infinity: easy to flip these by accident when copying code between a min and a max variant.

Assuming min/max support the same update tricks as sum: unlike sum, min and max are NOT invertible, meaning a min segment tree cannot support point updates via an "add a delta" style trick, an update must fully recompute by walking the standard build based ancestor chain instead.

Range Minimum Query is a foundational building block used inside harder problems. Sliding Window Maximum is a related but DIFFERENT problem more commonly solved with a monotonic deque rather than a segment tree, worth mentioning honestly that a segment tree is a valid but not the most efficient choice there.
